newsitem.title: FRANCE: Milosevic, Izetbegovic to meet on Balkan peace.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic, Izetbegovic to meet on Balkan peace.

text.p: Presidents Slobodan Milosevic of Serbia and Alija Izetbegovic of Bosnia meet in Paris on Thursday to consolidate improving relations and lay another brick in the wall shoring up the Dayton peace process.
Milosevic and Izetbegovic landed within minutes of each other, though at different airports, but made no statements.
They are scheduled to meet at 0800 GMT on Thursday before going into separate talks with French President Jacques Chirac.
Their talks are to focus on building peace after Bosnia's elections and normalising relations between the two countries, French officials said.
The three presidents will lunch together on Thursday joined by Carl Bildt, chief international civilian representative in Bosnia, and French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette.

Diplomats expect them to overcome their differences over Bosnia's lawsuit against Serbia and agree on a quick exchange of diplomatic missions -- almost one year late according to the Dayton timetable.
"It is likely the two presidents will agree to open missions in Belgrade and Sarajevo shortly," a senior western diplomat posted in Belgrade told Reuters.

The two presidents signed an agreement in Dayton, Ohio, last November recognizing each other's countries as sovereign states within current borders and agreed "urgently" to establish diplomatic relations and open embassies in respective capitals.
Sarajevo's lawsuit against Belgrade in March, 1993 before the Court of Justice in The Hague over alleged Serbian aggression against Bosnia has stalled the process, Serbian government sources say.
The former Yugoslav federal army supported the Bosnian Serbs when they rose against the Bosnian Moslem and Croat bid for independence in 1992.
It was the army guns that wrought havoc on Sarajevo killing 10,500 people and wounding another 50,000 when the Bosnian Serbs laid a three-year siege to the Bosnian capital.
But Serbia argues the army fell apart when Moslem and Croat officers defected and no Serbian officer remained in Bosnia to fight after the summer of 1992.
The open issue might force the two presidents to stop short of agreeing to open embassies and instead opt for only bureaux for the time being, diplomats said.
Belgrade told Sarajevo last Friday that diplomatic relations can not be established with the lawsuit still going on, but Bosnian officials said they would press the case.
Milosevic was instrumental in securing the Dayton peace accord by forcing recalcitrant Serb leaders to the negotiating table.
But his job did not end in Dayton and the West expects him to rein in Serb members of the future joint Bosnian government who pay lip service to Dayton while making no secret of separatist desires.

The West wants the three main players in the Balkan crisis -- Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia -- to normalise relations as soon as possible as a guarantee for stability in the Balkans and a deterrrent against any nationalist drives to break up Bosnia.
Yugoslavia and Croatia recognized each other on August 23.
"We want to see urgent, parallel and effective efforts at rebuilding peace in the Balkans and cannot afford to have too many loose ends for too long," the diplomat said.
